This is a picture of my FirstNet phone during a test — faster internet than most people’s cable or home Wi-Fi.

I’m a National Guardsman. I’ve deployed for emergencies and I’m ready to go again at a moment’s notice.

Every day I use FirstNet — the nationwide network built with AT&T — and it’s a game-changer. It’s faster and more reliable than regular AT&T plans. During disasters or training, it cuts straight through the congestion that kills everyone else’s signal. I get priority access and special features regular customers can’t buy.

Best part? I pay less out of pocket than regular plans. And it costs taxpayers nothing.

How is this possible?

After 9/11 showed how badly first responders needed better communication, Congress set up a smart public-private partnership. They gave AT&T dedicated spectrum and some existing auction money — not new taxes. AT&T poured in tens of billions of its own dollars to build a nationwide network. Today, first responders (police, firefighters, paramedics, nurses, doctors, and National Guardsmen like me) pay reasonable subscription fees that keep the whole thing running and upgrading itself. No annual bailouts. No government bureaucracy. Just reliable service when lives are on the line.

Why stop at phones?

We already have a proven model that works the exact same way for healthcare: TRICARE. In the same way FirstNet provides universal cell phone coverage across the United States, TRICARE already provides universal healthcare coverage as well!

Humana and other contractors run TRICARE for millions of military families and retirees. It delivers high-quality care through huge provider networks (including local ones like Main Line Health, CHOP, Penn Medicine, and Tower Health) at costs that are often a fraction of traditional Medicaid or many private plans. Programs like TRICARE Retired Reserve and [NAME] Adult already let families buy in on a cost-neutral, premium-based model — no cost to taxpayers.

Imagine scaling that same smart universal healthcare system nationwide to consumers the way AT&T scaled FirstNet. 

No new government takeover. No new taxes. Just let proven contractors compete — against Medicaid for public dollars and against insurance companies in the private market. Families could save at least $5,000 a year in premiums and out-of-pocket costs. Taxpayers could save billions. And we’d get better care that actually works when you need it most.

Critics say healthcare is “too complicated.” They said the same thing about emergency communications — until government contracting paradigms fixed it.

I’ve carried my FirstNet phone into the field and relied on TRICARE for my family during deployments. Both kept working when others didn't.

If we can do this for the phones that protect first responders and TRICARE programs that protect military families at zero net cost to taxpayers — why aren’t we doing it for every American family?

It’s time to stop treating healthcare like a political football and start treating it like the solvable problem it is.

FirstNet and TRICARE cost-neutral programs prove the model works.

How much could your family save? Check it out at VoteYoung.com

What do you think — should we bring this kind of proven, cost-saving approach to all Americans? Share if you agree.

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled,

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE; TABLE OF CONTENTS.

(a) Short Title.  This Act may be cited as the “Mental Health Access and Family Resilience Act” or “MHARA.”

SECTION 2. FINDINGS AND PURPOSE.

Congress finds the following:

(1) [NAME] families, faith communities, and personal responsibility form the foundation of mental resilience, as evidenced by reduced rates of depression, substance abuse, and suicide in stable family structures.

(2) Veterans, first responders, and residents in underserved communities, including Bexar County and Texas’s 20th Congressional District, face disproportionate mental health challenges, including PTSD, trauma from service, and economic stressors.

(3) Root causes such as family breakdown, substance abuse, gang violence, and limited community-based support must be addressed alongside clinical services.

(4) Expanding access to telehealth, peer support, and faith-informed counseling, while incentivizing private and local innovation, provides cost-effective, dignity-affirming care.

(5) Substance use disorders and mental health conditions frequently co-occur, exacerbating cycles of family breakdown, unemployment, and instability, particularly among veterans and in high-poverty areas like parts of Bexar County.

(6) Homelessness is often intertwined with untreated mental illness and substance abuse; stable housing paired with voluntary, family-centered treatment and personal accountability promotes long-term recovery and resilience.

The purpose of this Act is to enhance mental health access, build family resilience, and empower communities and veterans through targeted, accountable measures.

SECTION 3. DEFINITIONS.

(1) Family Resilience Programs: Evidence-based initiatives that strengthen marriage, parenting, and intergenerational support networks.

(2) Faith-Based Providers: Nonprofit organizations operating consistently with sincerely held religious beliefs that deliver mental health support.

(3) Veterans: Individuals who served in the uniformed services, as defined in section 101 of title 38, United States Code.

(4) Telehealth: Includes audio-visual and audio-only services compliant with HIPAA.

SECTION 4. EXPANDING ACCESS TO MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES.

(a) Medicaid and CHIP Flexibility. States may use Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program funds for intensive community-based mental health services, including peer support and family counseling, with emphasis on veterans and children.

(b) Telehealth Expansion. The Secretary of Health and Human Services shall extend and simplify telehealth coverage for mental health services in rural and underserved areas, including Texas districts, with parity for audio-only when clinically appropriate.

(c) Block Grants for Community Providers. Authorizes $20 million annually (subject to appropriations) in competitive grants to States and localities for community mental health clinics, prioritizing partnerships with veterans’ organizations, faith-based groups, and family-focused nonprofits.

SECTION 5. VETERANS AND FIRST RESPONDERS’ MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT.

(a) VA Peer Support Enhancement. Directs the Department of Veterans Affairs to expand peer-to-peer counseling programs, including the “Be There” program and veteran-serving organizations.

(b) Caregiver Support. Provides grants for caregiver mental health training and respite services for families of veterans with service-connected conditions.

(c) Law Enforcement and First Responders. Authorizes grants for officer wellness, peer support, and stigma-reduction programs modeled on successful bipartisan initiatives.

SECTION 6. FAMILY RESILIENCE AND PREVENTION.

(a) Family Strengthening Grants. Establishes a grant program through the Department of Health and Human Services for evidence-based programs that promote marriage education, parenting skills, and family counseling, with priority for high-poverty areas like parts of San Antonio.

(b) School-Based Family Partnerships. Encourages (without mandates) local educational agencies to partner with community organizations for voluntary family resilience workshops.

(c) Root Cause Initiatives. Supports data-driven programs addressing substance abuse, gang intervention, and fatherhood initiatives as preventive mental health measures.

SECTION 7. WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT AND PROVIDER TRAINING.

(a) Mental Health Workforce Grants. The Secretary of Health and Human Services shall establish a competitive grant program to States and eligible entities (including community colleges, veterans’ organizations, and faith-based institutions) to recruit, train, and retain mental health professionals, with priority for providers serving rural and underserved areas, veterans, and families.

(b) Training Emphasis. Grants shall support evidence-based training in trauma-informed care, family systems approaches, peer support, and integration of faith-based counseling where appropriate and consistent with provider's mission.

(c) Loan Repayment Incentives. Authorizes expansion of existing loan repayment programs for mental health providers committing to service in high-need districts, including Bexar County, Texas.

SECTION 8. SUICIDE PREVENTION AND CRISIS INTERVENTION.

(a) 988 Lifeline Enhancement. Directs the Secretary to strengthen the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline with improved routing to local, community, and faith-based responders.

(b) Veterans Suicide Prevention. Expands VA programs modeled on successful peer and community initiatives, including outreach to veterans’ families.

(c) Community Crisis Response. Authorizes grants for local crisis stabilization units and mobile response teams that prioritize de-escalation, family involvement, and diversion from hospitalization or incarceration.

SECTION 9. INTEGRATION WITH SUBSTANCE ABUSE PREVENTION AND TREATMENT.

(a) Co-Occurring Disorders Coordination. The Secretary of Health and Human Services, in coordination with the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, shall improve integration of mental health and substance use disorder services through joint funding opportunities, shared screening protocols, and care coordination models that prioritize evidence-based treatment for co-occurring conditions.

(b) Prevention and [NAME] Intervention. Authorizes grants to States and localities for community-based programs targeting root causes, including opioid misuse, methamphetamine, fentanyl, and alcohol abuse, with emphasis on veteran-specific outreach, family involvement, peer recovery coaches, and faith-based recovery support networks.

(c) Treatment and Recovery Expansion. Supports expansion of residential and outpatient treatment programs, including family-centered recovery options and incentives for long-term sobriety through job training and mentorship tied to personal responsibility.

(d) Veterans Focus. Directs the VA to enhance programs addressing substance use alongside PTSD and other service-related conditions, building on successful peer support and community reintegration models.

(e) Accountability Measures. Programs funded under this section shall emphasize measurable outcomes such as reduced relapse rates, family reunification, and decreased justice system involvement, with preference for providers demonstrating cost-effectiveness and voluntary participation.

SECTION 10. ADDRESSING HOMELESSNESS AS A MENTAL HEALTH AND FAMILY STABILITY PRIORITY.

(a) Housing-First with Treatment Integration. Authorizes competitive grants to local governments, veterans’ organizations, faith-based nonprofits, and community providers for supportive housing programs that combine stable housing with voluntary mental health and substance abuse treatment, prioritizing veterans, families, and individuals with co-occurring disorders.

(b) Local Innovation and Accountability. Grants shall favor evidence-based approaches that encourage personal responsibility, family reunification where appropriate, and partnerships with job training and life-skills programs. Nothing in this section shall mandate Housing First models that de-emphasize treatment or enable ongoing substance abuse.

(c) Veterans and Family Emphasis. Expands eligibility and funding flexibility for VA and HUD programs serving homeless veterans with mental health needs, including caregiver support and transitional housing that strengthens family units. Prioritizes projects in high-need districts such as TX-20.

(d) Crisis Diversion and Prevention. Supports mobile outreach teams, crisis stabilization centers, and rapid rehousing initiatives that divert individuals from streets or emergency rooms into treatment and housing pathways, with strong coordination between mental health providers, law enforcement, and community organizations.

(e) Reporting and Safeguards. Recipients must report on outcomes including housing stability, treatment engagement, reduced recidivism to homelessness, and cost savings. Protects religious liberty for faith-based providers and prohibits the use of funds to promote or enable illegal drug use.

SECTION 11. YOUTH AND SCHOOL-BASED FAMILY PARTNERSHIPS.

(a) Voluntary Programs. Encourages local educational agencies to partner with families and community organizations for voluntary mental health education, resilience-building, and parental involvement workshops.

(b) Child and Adolescent Focus. Authorizes targeted grants for early intervention services emphasizing family stability, avoiding ideological approaches, and protecting parental rights.

(c) No Mandates. Nothing in this section shall be construed to impose new requirements on schools or infringe on local control or parental authority.

SECTION 12. RESEARCH, INNOVATION, AND DATA COLLECTION.

(a) Evidence-Based Research. Directs the National Institutes of Health, in coordination with the Department of Veterans Affairs, to prioritize research on family resilience factors, faith-informed interventions, and cost-effective community models.

(b) Outcome Metrics. Requires standardized data collection on program effectiveness, focusing on reduced suicide rates, hospitalizations, substance use, and improved family stability indicators.

(c) Innovation Grants. Establishes limited demonstration projects for novel local solutions, with rigorous evaluation and sunset after 3 years.

SECTION 13. ACCOUNTABILITY, OVERSIGHT, AND REPORTING.

(a) Reporting Requirements. The Secretary of HHS and the Secretary of VA shall submit annual reports to Congress on outcomes, including metrics on reduced hospitalizations, suicide rates, and family stability indicators.

(b) Sunset Provision. This Act shall expire after 5 years unless reauthorized, ensuring fiscal responsibility.

(c) No New Entitlements. Nothing in this Act shall be construed to create an individual entitlement to services.

SECTION 14. AUTHORIZATION OF APPROPRIATIONS.

There are authorized to be appropriated such sums as may be necessary to carry out this Act for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, with amounts allocated across sections subject to annual appropriations and oversight to ensure fiscal responsibility.

SECTION 15. EFFECTIVE DATE; SUNSET PROVISION.

(a) This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.
